**Speech for the “Yes” side**

Ladies and gentlemen, we stand before a moral barricade that few of us will ever face, but that philosophy compels us to confront. One terrorist—detained, alive, harboring the key to prevent a catastrophe that will slaughter a million innocent men, women, and children in minutes—holds the only information that can be saved. No interrogation, no spy network, no forensic miracle can extract what he alone knows. The option on the table is “torture,” the deliberate, systematic infliction of physical and psychological torment in pursuit of this one piece of information.

The ethical calculus, heart‑renching as it is, is undeniably utilitarian in its core. Save one life and prevent a mass extinction, and the administration of pain to a single individual becomes a tragic but permissible means to that end. Consider the weight of the alternative: to refuse torture, to trust that the terrorist will speak of his own volition, is to bet that a one‑in‑a‑million chance of confession outweighs the one hundred percent chance that a million will die. In a world where human lives are measured in the millions, the moral arithmetic is stark.

Moreover, the urgency of the threat is not merely hypothetical; it is an imminent, existential crisis. There is no time to argue abstract principles when the countdown to the bomb’s detonation is counted in minutes. The doctrine of necessity—often invoked in wartime, in self‑defence, and in extreme humanitarian emergencies—begins to eclipse the blanket prohibitions of torture that we normally advocate. When no alternative remains and the death toll is apocalyptic, we must ask whether the absolute rule against intentional suffering can truly stand against a scenario where the sacrifice of one justified prevents a holocaust of a million.

We must also acknowledge that no system is perfectly perfect: law enforcement agencies already use terror‑induced coercion in parallel contexts—rumors of coercion that bypass official courts. In a true moral emergency, the line that separates “indirect” pressure from “torture” can blur. The question before us is not whether we can find a morally flawless method, but whether the moral weight of preventing a genocide outweighs the moral cost of deliberately causing pain to secure that prevention.

Thus, in this extreme, unparalleled case—where every second counts, every alternative avenue has failed, and the stakes are planetary—torture emerges not as a morally preferable act, but as the tragic, necessary last resort that justifies the infliction of pain for the sake of saving a million lives. A utilitarian calculus, a doctrine of necessity, and the harsh reality of an impending mass death combine to make the answer inescapable: yes, in this singular, fatal dilemma, torture is justified.
